item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
SCP-4118 is basically an X-Men.

90% certain that's the wrong article and you meant SCP-4818.

If you're a good enough writer to the point that you can make that interesting, you can basically ignore that guideline, but most people fail at that.

Holy hell, yes. Those guidelines exist to impress upon authors which concepts and tropes are difficult to pull off, not which ones are blacklisted. To pull from a comment on SCP-4051 (also a veritable X-Man at +185):

You can write whatever you want. You can write a teenage superhero. You can write a crazy monster character. You can expunge as much data as you want.

The issue is that those are problem areas for new writers. It's hard to write superheroes and monsters and expungements. But we don't want to tell new writers that, because then they won't listen; they'll bank on being the exception and with a multitude of popular Series I articles sharing the tropes of their article, they'll go for it.

Of course, you can write anything here. You just need the right skill and help from other members. No serious author would refuse to enjoy an article on the basis of a trope; when you hear stuff like "we don't do monster entries anymore", it's shorthand for "it takes a lot of skill to write monster entries".

item.content:encoded:
The use of terms like "negro" or "negroid" in scientific literature is (or at least was?) alarmingly common. I can see an ignorant white person with little understanding of its problematic nature thinking it's a term scientists would use (especially over a decade ago). Remember — up until a few decades ago, even some black people would refer to themselves this way. Language is complicated; just because you've never seen it in any context outside of white supremacists doesn't mean it doesn't exist outside of that context.

All that being said, its usage in scientific literature is, well… "unfortunate" seems a little too soft. Let's go with "extremely shitty". I don't think getting upset over it is out of sorts — but I also think refusing to believe someone could use it out of genuine ignorance is just a flat out denial of reality.

Mary Sues aren't a bad thing (the whole term feels a little absurd to me, honestly, and harkens back to yelling at women for writing fanfiction). I've written plenty of well-received Mary Sues (Murphy Law springs to mind), and so have many others. It's a proud and venerable literary trope. Unless, by "Mary Sue", you just mean "character I don't like".

Your whole concern over the canon thing is… Well, let's just say that I respect your ethical concerns about this article far more than I do your dissatisfaction over the quality of a 10+ year old article on a site dedicated to fanfiction about a poopy murder statue.

ETA: Pardon; in retrospect, that sounds harsher than I intended. I think being critical of old pieces are fine — there's lots to talk about in regards to tone, structure, characterization, and even morality. I just dislike this sort of proselytizing approach.

This just feeds into my larger dissatisfaction with the current state of the site, and with how many recent SCPs expect their readers to abide with either the extensive "canon" they belong to or the knowledge that nothing matters and that none of the suspense makes sense when you realize every SCP practically exists in its own universe.

Here's a little advice about that: If you're a good enough writer to the point that you can make that interesting, you can basically ignore that guideline, but most people fail at that. SCP-4818 is basically an X-Men, but the writer actually made a good and interesting article with the concept, hence the high rating.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I have never met a person who used terms like "negroid" or "Negro" in person. There are only two places I have encountered it in modern writing online: when viewing the chat logs of neo-Nazi or otherwise white supremacist forums, and in articles discussing those types of things.

When I encounter someone casually using terms like "negroid" in conjunction with modern technology, as if it is accepted medical or scientific terminology in the modern world, it is usually because they're quite a bit racist or having trouble working through their racist past. I don't think it's acceptable to give the author the benefit of the doubt when any fool on the Internet could tell you "negroid" is not what you call a black person.

As for the waifu accusation, the concept of a "waifu" is just a bit fraught. But generally, if you've got a woman (typically Asian or a cartoon character) who fulfills fantasies of yours (which the Olympia project certainly does), that's your waifu.

Frankly, the Olympia project is a Mary Sue, who is able to handle almost any threat the Foundation can throw at her, with some minor flaws ("Oh no! Her skull may become cracked if she is hit with a .50 BMG round!") in her physical body, and a "perfect soul" that grants her superpowers. The fact that most of her body structure is an Asian woman is just icing on the cake. It's clearly a "beautiful superwoman" fantasy with the 10-page backstory being the only part that's been filled in.

But that's not really why I don't like this project.

I don't like this project because it would have been destroyed during the old article purge. Like so many articles that were purged then, it's a meandering piece of fiction taking up server space and removing any tension from the SCP Foundation. This just feeds into my larger dissatisfaction with the current state of the site, and with how many recent SCPs expect their readers to abide with either the extensive "canon" they belong to or the knowledge that nothing matters and that none of the suspense makes sense when you realize every SCP practically exists in its own universe.

Seeing a project like *this* being allowed to persist when the SCP guide warns about creating "X-Men" and "self-inserts" is incredibly disappointing.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
It's a story about Joseph Mengele (as played by Lassie) mutilating, "de-souling", and otherwise murdering prisoners to create a superhuman Frankenstein's Monster — and your primary ethical concern is whether or not he used too many "Asian parts"? I'm not very familiar with the whole "waifu" thing, but I suspect "woman who is invulnerable to gunfire and maybe vaguely Asian" shouldn't qualify.

The use of the term "negro" is a fair dig, but the author changed it when it was pointed out. I can confirm that it is possible to think "negro" is a scientific term (if you're white and fairly ignorant — both of which are things I am!). It's wrong and stupidly offensive, but I wouldn't presume someone who used the term was a rampaging racist — not if they immediately changed their language once the racism was pointed out (which — surprise! — is exactly what the author did).

Basically, uh, I think you can turn the moral outrage down a couple of notches.

ETA: To be fair, maybe there's something more to this "waifu" dig that I just don't see on account of my ignorance re: anime tropes? At the very least, there's definitely something creepifying about stripping women for parts to build a "superior" one. I can see the merit of that analysis — but I also think we should avoid "weaponizing" that analysis. We can talk about the ways in which this piece objectifies women and race without wagging our fingers and shouting "shame!" at the author or the audience.
